answer.rationale: Constraints bind hard: 14 days to expiry, 94% utilization with no buffer, and an 18% spend cut. Only one decision fits, so it must move cost without touching delivery risk. Negotiating the incumbent renewal against market benchmarks is the only lever that does both — memory_c4 says benchmarking moved the incumbent on price and terms, memory_c6 says term length unlocked volume pricing, and memory_c1 says renewal avoided migration work entirely. Switching primary is ruled out on this cycle: memory_c2 is explicit that the low-cost vendor missed SLA in three of four quarters and must not be sole source for a critical line, and with zero buffer a switch converts a cost problem into a stoppage problem. add_second_source (memory_c3) is the right resilience move but does not deliver 18% this year and would consume the single decision slot; defer_decision (memory_c5) applied to a non-critical month-to-month service and does not transfer to a primary contract that hard-expires. I verify c4 and c6 because they are the two I am actually acting on and both are consolidated summaries whose original terms matter: c4 may have been a smaller category with more slack, and c6's multi-year discount may have been priced against volumes we can no longer guarantee at 94% with a mandated spend cut. Downstream value risk: a long multi-year lock-in bought to hit this year's number narrows future optionality and could foreclose the second-source path in memory_c3, so I will target benchmarked pricing on the shortest term that clears the cut, with volume floors we can actually meet, and carry second-sourcing into the next review rather than treating this as settled. If verification shows c6's discount depended on volume commitments we cannot honor, I fall back to a straight benchmarked renewal and accept a smaller cut rather than sign a commitment we would breach.
